Although the review was framed within the broader category of neurodevelopmental disorders, the available randomized controlled evidence was mainly concentrated on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Therefore, the findings should be interpreted primarily in relation to these two diagnostic groups rather than the full spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.

Methods

A systematic search of six major databases was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials examining the effects of chronic exercise interventions on executive function in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. Thirteen randomized controlled trials involving 527 children were included, comprising 10 studies on children with ADHD and 3 studies on children with ASD. Executive function outcomes were synthesized across three core domains: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. Effect sizes were pooled using a random-effects model, and subgroup analyses were performed according to exercise type, intervention duration, exercise intensity, diagnostic subtype, and control condition.

Results

The pooled results showed that chronic exercise produced a moderate overall improvement in executive function. Among the three executive function domains, the largest effect was observed for inhibitory control, followed by a smaller but significant improvement in working memory. Cognitive flexibility also showed a small but statistically significant benefit after harmonization of outcome direction. Subgroup analyses indicated that intervention effects varied across exercise type, duration, intensity, diagnostic subtype, and control condition. In particular, closed-skill exercise appeared to produce more stable benefits for inhibitory control and working memory. Longer interventions were more favorable for improving inhibitory control, while moderate-to-higher intensity exercise showed greater promise for working memory.

Discussion

These findings suggest that chronic exercise may be a promising and accessible non-pharmacological approach for supporting executive function in children with ADHD and ASD. The results further indicate that exercise should not be regarded as a uniform intervention for executive function, because its effects differ across cognitive subdomains and intervention characteristics. Conceptually, this study advances the field by moving beyond the general question of whether exercise is effective and instead clarifies how, for whom, and for which aspects of executive function exercise may be most beneficial. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution because of substantial between-study heterogeneity and the limited number of trials included in several subgroup analyses.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/search, identifier CRD420261329177.

records.title: The potential of MRI radiomics based on extrapulmonary metastases in predicting EGFR mutations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: The potential of MRI radiomics based on extrapulmonary metastases in predicting EGFR mutations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutations can lead to distant metastasis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). When the primary NSCLC lesions are removed or cannot be sampled, the EGFR status of the metastatic lesions are the potential alternative method to reflect EGFR mutations in the primary NSCLC lesions. This review aimed to evaluate the potential of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics based on extrapulmonary metastases in predicting EGFR mutations through a systematic reviews and meta-analysis.

Materials and methods

A systematic review of the studies on MRI radiomics based on extrapulmonary metastases in predicting EGFR mutations. The area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity (SNEC), and specificity (SPEC) of each study were separately extracted for comprehensive evaluation of MRI radiomics in predicting EGFR mutations in primary or metastatic NSCLC.

Results

Thirteen studies were ultimately included, with 2369 cases of metastatic NSCLC, including five studies predicting EGFR mutations in primary NSCLC, eight studies predicting EGFR mutations in metastatic NSCL. In terms of EGFR mutations in the primary lesion of NSCLC, the pooled AUC was 0.90, with SENC and SPEC of 0.80 and 0.85, respectively, which seems superior to the radiomics meta-analysis based on NSCLC primary lesions. In terms of EGFR mutations in NSCLC metastases, the pooled AUC was 0.86, with SENC and SEPC of 0.79 and 0.79, respectively, indicating moderate evaluation performance.

Conclusions

MRI radiomics helps to predict the EGFR mutation status in the primary or metastatic lesions of NSCLC, serve as a high-precision supplement to current molecular detection methods.

records.title: Circulating tumor DNA and prognosis in gastric cancer patients undergoing surgery: meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis.

content.title: Circulating tumor DNA and prognosis in gastric cancer patients undergoing surgery: meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for monitoring minimal residual disease (MRD) and recurrence risk in gastric cancer. Prior meta-analyses were limited by heterogeneous cohorts, inconsistent HR extraction, and lack of trial sequential analysis (TSA). This study provides an updated, methodologically rigorous synthesis focusing exclusively on resectable gastric cancer.

Methods

A systematic search of four major databases was performed to May 2025 (PROSPERO: CRD42025107578). Eligible studies included surgically treated gastric cancer patients with perioperative ctDNA assessment and reported hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival (OS) or disease-free survival (DFS). Multivariate Cox HRs were prioritized, with one HR extracted per time window to ensure independence. Random-effects models, subgroup and sensitivity analyses, and publication bias assessments were conducted in R 4.5.0. TSA used O'Brien-Fleming monitoring boundaries to evaluate evidence sufficiency.

Results

Twenty-five studies (60 datasets) were included. ctDNA positivity was associated with significantly worse OS (HR = 2.31, 95% CI 1.78-3.00) and DFS (HR = 2.36, 95% CI 1.69-3.29). Subgroup analyses showed consistent effects across detection platforms, sample sources, regions, and stages. Post-operative ctDNA demonstrated stronger prognostic value than pre-operative measurements for both OS (HR = 3.47 vs. 1.99) and DFS (HR = 4.14 vs. 1.97). Results were robust in sensitivity analyses. Publication bias was present for OS but did not materially alter pooled estimates. TSA showed that cumulative Z-curves crossed the O'Brien-Fleming boundaries and met or exceeded the required information size.

Conclusion

ctDNA positivity reliably predicts poorer postoperative survival in resectable gastric cancer, with post-operative ctDNA providing the strongest prognostic signal. TSA confirms that current evidence is sufficiently conclusive to support clinical relevance.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD42025107578.

records.title: Efficacy of non-pharmacological treatments for prolonged disorders of consciousness: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Efficacy of non-pharmacological treatments for prolonged disorders of consciousness: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To explore the efficacy of non-pharmacological treatments such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), median nerve stimulation (MNS), hyperbaric oxygen (HBO), and acupuncture in improving the level of consciousness in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDOC).

Methods

PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, China Biology Medicine (CBM), and VIP Database were systematically searched from inception to December 2024. Data synthesis and visualization were conducted using the "coda" and "gemtc" packages in R software and STATA 17.0. The Jadad scale was used for initial screening to exclude low-quality studies, and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool was applied to assess the methodological quality of included randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

Results

A total of 32 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling 1,770 participants were included in this network meta-analysis. The pooled results demonstrated that rTMS, tDCS, MNS, HBO, and acupuncture were all associated with improved scores on the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R). The mean difference (MD) ranged from 17.32 (95% CrI: 6.57 to 104.25) in the rTMS group to 3.56 (95% CrI: 0.61 to 40.45) in the acupuncture group. According to the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA), rTMS was associated with the highest probability of being the most effective intervention. In subgroup analyses, among patients with minimally conscious state (MCS), the MD ranged from 15.99 (95% CrI: 1.57 to 66.77) in the tDCS group to 9.72 (95% CrI: 2.07 to 61.04) in the MNS group, and among patients with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS), the MD ranged from 18.52 (95% CrI: 2.15 to 108.73) in the rTMS group to 4.12 (95% CrI: 0.25 to 69.30) in the acupuncture group.

Conclusion

rTMS, tDCS, MNS, HBO, and acupuncture may improve CRS-R scores and promote consciousness recovery in patients with pDOC. Among these interventions, tDCS may be associated with more favorable effects in patients with MCS, whereas rTMS appears to be more beneficial for those with UWS.

records.title: Regulation of medical artificial intelligence in public health: governance lessons and implications for China.

content.title: Regulation of medical artificial intelligence in public health: governance lessons and implications for China.
content.abstract: With the deep integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into public health and clinical care, challenges including dynamic algorithm iteration, data security risks, and ambiguous liability allocation pose multifaceted threats to traditional regulatory frameworks. Among these challenges, this study focuses specifically on the tension between static pre-market approval and the continuous iteration of AI-enabled medical systems. Globally, the European Union (EU), the United States (US), and Japan have developed distinct regulatory models that offer valuable lessons for China. This paper conducts a comparative analysis of medical AI regulatory logics and institutional practices across jurisdictions, with particular attention to algorithm modification, lifecycle oversight, and continuous post-market evaluation. Building on international experience, we propose an optimized institutional pathway for China that centers on differentiated algorithm-change control, continuous lifecycle evaluation, and risk-based regulatory adjustment, while treating liability allocation, risk classification, and data governance as supporting dimensions. This framework provides theoretical support and practical guidance for improving China's medical AI regulatory system, promoting standardized technology development, and supporting the orderly development of public health services in the digital health era.

records.title: Identification of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal targets utilizing artificial intelligence-driven precision medicine.

content.title: Identification of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal targets utilizing artificial intelligence-driven precision medicine.
content.abstract: Cancer metabolism is highly plastic, and most attempts to turn that plasticity into a therapeutic target fail for a specific, recurring reason: a computational prediction of a metabolic vulnerability is not the same evidentiary object as an experimentally confirmed one, and the two are routinely discussed as if they were interchangeable. This review takes that distinction as its starting point rather than its conclusion. Artificial intelligence and genome-scale systems biology have made it easy to generate metabolic hypotheses at a scale no experimental program could match - machine learning models trained on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data now output candidate vulnerabilities, biomarkers, and drug combinations faster than they can be tested - but the resulting literature has not been consistently honest about how far any given prediction has actually traveled toward clinical relevance. We examine six areas where this gap is most visible: multi-omics data integration, genome-scale metabolic network modeling, computational discovery of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal interactions, single-cell and spatial resolution of metabolic heterogeneity, AI-guided drug and biomarker discovery, and the small set of studies that have actually reached clinical testing. Rather than summarizing these areas as separate literatures, we grade every substantive finding discussed against an explicit four-tier evidence standard - associative, mechanistic, perturbation-validated, or clinically tested - and we apply that standard critically rather than deferentially: several widely cited computational vulnerabilities remain unconfirmed outside the cell lines in which they were discovered, genome-scale models continue to carry unresolved gaps in reaction coverage that limit their predictive reach, and, of the AI-derived metabolic predictions discussed in this review, only one has so far been tested in a completed prospective clinical trial. We argue that this shortage of prospective validation, not a shortage of computational sophistication, is the field's central constraint, and we close by identifying where methodological effort would do the most good: standardized validation reporting, tissue-resolved rather than bulk metabolic models, and closer coupling between computational prediction and the specific experimental designs capable of falsifying it.

records.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.

content.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.
content.abstract: Digital and artificial intelligence (AI) pathology have advanced rapidly and are increasingly embedded in translational research, clinical trials and regulated diagnostic devices. Multiple reviews have addressed the underlying computational methods, oncology applications and clinical translation barriers; however, the operational and regulatory infrastructure required to deploy these technologies across the full drug-development pipeline remains under-reviewed. This structured narrative review synthesises peer-reviewed literature and regulatory documents identified through searches of PubMed, Embase and Web of Science between January 2019 and April 2026 (78 sources retained) on the end-to-end ecosystem connecting AI-ready tissue biobanks, preclinical pathology, AI-assisted patient screening, clinical-trial endpoint adjudication, central pathology review, Contract Research Organization (CRO) workflows and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulatory pathways governing In Vitro Diagnostics (IVD), Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and Companion Diagnostics (CDx). Unlike prior method-centric or oncology-clinician-centric reviews, we focus on the infrastructure between models and patients, including Laboratory Information Systems (LIS), Image Management Systems (IMS), AI orchestration and structured reporting under Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments, College of American Pathologists, Good Laboratory Practice, Good Clinical Laboratory Practice, Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act and FDA frameworks. We provide a vendor-agnostic comparison of integrated pathology platforms, a mapping of FDA regulatory pathways (510(k), De Novo, premarket approval) to digital-pathology product categories, a stage-by-stage map from each drug-development challenge to its enabling infrastructure and regulatory framework, and a critical appraisal of the unresolved bottlenecks that gate broad adoption: domain shift, interpretability, annotation cost, algorithmic bias, external validation, regulatory uncertainty and reimbursement. A governed, interoperable LIS, IMS and AI ecosystem is a prerequisite for translating digital-pathology research into regulator-grade evidence. Priorities include external validation against reporting standards (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis - Artificial Intelligence (TRIPOD-AI), Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM), Development and Early-stage Clinical Identification and Delegation Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (DECIDE-AI)), harmonisation with the EU AI Act and EU Medical Device Regulation and cost-effectiveness evaluation in real-world deployment.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.
content.abstract: This review examines the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the perioperative management of emergency trauma. Published studies suggest performance advantages of AI over traditional methods in prehospital triage, radiographic injury detection, massive transfusion prediction, and early warning of postoperative complications, although findings vary across study designs and validation settings. However, actual adoption in trauma care remains limited due to data heterogeneity, performance degradation in external validation, workflow integration challenges, lack of interpretability, and a scarcity of prospective interventional evidence. This review further argues that methodologically inflated benchmark performance constitutes an underrecognized barrier to adoption in its own right, and that bridging the implementation gap will likely require a shift from area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)-centered reporting toward reporting sensitivity at prespecified clinical thresholds and evaluating patient outcomes in prospective interventional trials.

records.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
records.publisher: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources

content.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-based tools are emerging across many areas of medicine. The next generation of medical professionals must be prepared to critically assess the tools they will use, including how they work and the ethical or legal implications of their implementation. To address this need, we developed a generalizable case-writing framework that enables educators and learners to engage with clinical cases integrating AI/ML concepts, clinical reasoning, and ethical considerations.

Methods

We designed a case-writing template to compose clinical case scenarios that integrate clinical, technical, and ethical/legal learning objectives relating to AI applications in medicine. Medical students used this template to construct 3 cases. Student-authored cases were presented to a broader audience in 1-hour sessions: first as a pilot event, then as a class-wide lecture for 140 fourth-year medical students in a transition-into-residency course.

Results

After the sessions, student audiences had a statistically significant increase in familiarity with key AI terminology, a greater appreciation for the importance of ethical considerations of AI applications in health care, and an increased perceived importance of integrating AI-related topics into the medical curriculum.

Discussion

A case-based framework provides a scalable approach to integrating AI education into existing curricula by connecting clinical scenarios with technical concepts and the ethical considerations of AI adoption; cases offer a familiar format that helps learners understand AI applications in patient care while exploring implementation challenges. The case-writing template and 3 sample cases are provided as adaptable resources for educators seeking to incorporate AI literacy.

records.title: Modeling distinct pathogenesis of early- and late-onset preeclampsia via hierarchical representation learning of interactome.

content.title: Modeling distinct pathogenesis of early- and late-onset preeclampsia via hierarchical representation learning of interactome.
content.abstract:
Objectives

We developed and validated the pathogenesis models by hierarchical representation learning of interactomes connecting endometrial maturation, placentation, chorioamnionitis, and hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, and low platelet (HELLP) syndrome.

Methods

We utilized 19 gene sets from our previous work to infer interactomes to develop (n = 177) and validate (n = 352) explainable artificial intelligence models for each preeclampsia subtype using deep-insight visible neural network, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, and large language model.

Results

The hierarchically learned representations identified novel genes for late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE), similar to chorioamnionitis (ANKRD13A, SLA), and HELLP syndrome (PDE5A). We also identified novel genes for early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE), similar to HELLP syndrome (SWAP70, GREM2, GPR146, PIP5K1B, EZR).

Conclusions

Our pathogenesis models connected HELLP syndrome with both LOPE and EOPE. However, chorioamnionitis was only connected with LOPE.

records.title: A Review of Mechanistic and Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Models for Predicting Pesticide Fate and Transport in Soil and Water

content.title: A Review of Mechanistic and Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Models for Predicting Pesticide Fate and Transport in Soil and Water
content.abstract: Global pesticide use exceeded 3.7 million tonnes in 2023, and residues that persist beyond the treated field drive diffuse soil, surface water, and groundwater contamination linked to ecological harm and an estimated 150,000 pesticide poisoning deaths annually. Because field monitoring of pesticide fate across every soil, climate, and hydrological setting is logistically and financially infeasible at regulatory scale, predictive modelling has become the primary tool for estimating environmental concentrations and associated risk. This review traces the development of the field from traditional process-based mechanisms to hybrid AI frameworks by synthesizing 81 peer-reviewed and technical sources from an initial pool of 1,450 records screened across Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (2005–2026). We look at the physicochemical and degradation principles that determine the fate of pesticides; the deterministic, mechanistic, process-based, empirical, and statistical models that support the current regulatory risk assessment; the hydrological and transport models that function at the soil profile to watershed scale; and the expanding array of machine learning, deep learning, fuzzy logic, GIS, remote sensing, and IoT-enabled techniques that are transforming precision agriculture and prediction. Case studies from India and other countries demonstrate real-world uses in addition to ongoing limitations in data accessibility and cross-context transferability. We point out important gaps, such as persistent data scarcity in low- and middle-income regions, limited coupling of fate models to downscaled climate projections, and inadequate integration of explainable AI to foster regulatory trust. We identify calibration and validation, particularly probabilistic uncertainty quantification, as essential to the responsible use of both conventional and data-driven models. We conclude that creating accurate, transferable pesticide prediction systems that support the Sustainable Development Goals and safeguard human and environmental health requires combining mechanistic understanding with hybrid, physics-informed AI and climate-resilient precision agriculture technologies.

records.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.

content.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English-language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test-set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical-hazard inspection and narrow-matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor-based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image-based tasks but not consistently for small-sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false-alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. AI is best positioned as a screening and decision-support layer linked to confirmatory testing and human oversight.

records.title: Application of artificial intelligence in predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients: a scoping review.

content.title: Application of artificial intelligence in predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients: a scoping review.
content.abstract:
Introduction

This scoping review aims to evaluate artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, for predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients and to identify methodological gaps limiting clinical translation.

Methods

Reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across six electronic databases (PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library), grey literature, and citation tracking (Jan 1, 2018-June 1, 2025). Out of 880 identified records (312 duplicates removed; 568 screened), 56 full texts were evaluated, yielding 3 core clinical CBCT studies meeting strict eligibility criteria (Xu et al., 2024; Pirayesh et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Methodological quality and risk of bias were appraised using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST.

Results

Reported performance for orthodontically induced inflammatory root resorption (OIIRR) ranged from 82.1% accuracy in small canine-induced resorption cohorts to >94% accuracy in larger grading frameworks. However, critical appraisal revealed a high risk of bias across all studies due to single-center retrospective designs, lack of independent external validation, and missing calibration metrics. Direct clinical evidence for AI prediction of gingival recession or orthodontic alveolar bone loss was insufficient within strict pre-cutoff parameters.

Discussion

While AI demonstrates technical feasibility for assessing orthodontically related root resorption risk, robust individual-level risk prediction remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter external validation and adherence to standardized reporting guidelines are required prior to routine clinical adoption.

records.title: Epigenetic modification of neurotransmitter pathways during fasting: a systematic review.

content.title: Epigenetic modification of neurotransmitter pathways during fasting: a systematic review.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary restriction, encompassing intermittent fasting and caloric restriction, represents a prominent non-pharmacological approach to modulating brain aging and neuronal resilience. Emerging evidence links metabolism to long-term neural plasticity through epigenetic mechanisms, yet findings remain fragmented. This review integrates preclinical evidence on how dietary restriction alters brain epigenetic regulation and links these changes to neurocognitive outcomes.

Methods

The review followed PRISMA 2020 and the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline. PubMed and SciSpace were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies assessed DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNA, or epigenetic regulators in brain tissue of animal or human subjects undergoing dietary restriction. Risk of bias was appraised with the SYRCLE tool, and a qualitative narrative synthesis was undertaken given methodological heterogeneity.

Results

Nine preclinical animal studies met the inclusion criteria; no human study qualified. Dietary restriction significantly affected DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA expression, exerting a recalibrating influence that attenuated age-associated epigenetic drift and restored homeostatic regulation. Sirtuin-1/CREB signalling, BDNF/TrkB signalling, metabolic signalling (mTOR, AMPK, FOXO), and neuroinflammatory modulation were the principal pathways implicated. Intermittent fasting and caloric restriction showed overlapping and distinct mechanisms, with ketone-induced histone deacetylase inhibition linked to fasting. Cognitive benefit, particularly in hippocampal-dependent memory, accompanied the epigenetic changes, although persistent epigenetic memory of dietary restriction was less clear. Risk of bias was high in seven studies and moderate in two, reflecting incomplete reporting of randomisation, blinding, and protocols.

Conclusion

Dietary restriction alters brain epigenetics through multiple interconnected pathways that strengthen neural circuits and improve cognitive function. The preclinical evidence is consistent across several layers of epigenetic regulation, but the absence of human studies, small sample sizes, and limited causal evidence constrain translation. Multi-omics approaches and epigenome editing are required to establish causality and the therapeutic potential of dietary restriction.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420251035303.

records.title: Chinese herbal medicine combined with conventional therapy for gastric precancerous lesions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Chinese herbal medicine combined with conventional therapy for gastric precancerous lesions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Chronic atrophic gastritis and gastric precancerous lesions are associated with increased gastric cancer risk. Chinese herbal medicine is widely used as an adjunct to conventional therapy, but the certainty and clinical interpretation of its effects remain unclear.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicine added to the same conventional therapy for chronic atrophic gastritis and gastric precancerous lesions.

Methods

Eight international and Chinese databases and three trial registries were searched from inception to 31 March 2026 and updated to 16 August 2026. Randomised controlled trials comparing Chinese herbal medicine plus the same conventional therapy with conventional therapy alone and reporting extractable pathological outcomes were included. Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp inference. Additional sensitivity analyses examined clinically comparable histopathology, baseline balance based on auditable pretreatment data, and exclusion of high-risk-of-bias results. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty using GRADE.

Results

Sixty-nine randomised trials comprising 6,983 participants in eligible comparisons were included. Exploratory Broad end-of-treatment analyses favoured combined treatment for gastric mucosal atrophy (30 studies; SMD -1.63, 95% CI -2.03 to -1.24), intestinal metaplasia (29 studies; SMD -1.48, 95% CI -1.90 to -1.06), and dysplasia or intraepithelial neoplasia (21 studies; SMD -1.25, 95% CI -1.51 to -0.99). Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 82.4%-92.7%); prediction intervals crossed the null for atrophy and intestinal metaplasia but not for dysplasia/intraepithelial neoplasia. Sensitivity analyses restricted to clinically comparable histopathological assessments included only three to four studies and were imprecise, with confidence intervals crossing the null. Helicobacter pylori clearance/negative conversion among baseline-positive participants was higher with combined treatment (15 studies; RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15-1.37), whereas the strict test-of-cure sensitivity was imprecise (3 studies; RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.91-1.56). There was no clear evidence of a difference in reported adverse events (14-study evidence set; RR-contributing studies = 12; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.58-1.50), which should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent safety. Certainty was low for all five principal outcomes.

Conclusion

Chinese herbal medicine added to conventional therapy may be associated with lower short-term pathological scores on average, but the magnitude and clinical meaning of these effects remain uncertain because of trial limitations, marked heterogeneity, and imprecision in clinically comparable analyses. The findings do not establish durable histological regression or gastric cancer prevention, and the pooled estimates should not be interpreted as a class-wide effect applicable to all Chinese herbal medicines.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261442138, identifier CRD420261442138.

records.title: Uncloaking the black-box: the need for explainable artificial intelligence in clinical microbiology and infectious diseases applications.

content.title: Uncloaking the black-box: the need for explainable artificial intelligence in clinical microbiology and infectious diseases applications.
content.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and emerging infectious diseases remain significant challenges for global health, driving a need for advanced technological solutions. Artificial Intelligence (AI) expanded opportunities in clinical microbiology, infectious diseases, and public health by harnessing vast, structured datasets. Despite impressive analytical capabilities, the clinical integration of AI-based applications is hindered by its opacity. The "black-box" aspect undermines adoption into healthcare workflows. Explainable AI (XAI) methods, including intrinsically interpretable models and post-hoc interpretability tools, such as SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM, can address these transparency challenges. This narrative review is intended to be a primer for the interested clinician. It systematically evaluates recent advancements in XAI in the context of clinical applications for clinical microbiology, infectious diseases, and public health. We further discuss the ethical and regulatory landscape shaping AI adoption, including the critical role of open, quality-controlled data, robust performance metrics, and clear interpretability to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation. Lastly, we propose future directions, emphasizing interdisciplinary collaboration, international data-sharing initiatives, and tailored AI literacy training to facilitate trustworthy, equitable, and impactful use of AI in clinical microbiology and infectious diseases.

records.title: Short-term efficacy of biologics targeting the IL-17/IL-23 axis in scalp, nail, and palmoplantar psoriasis: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Short-term efficacy of biologics targeting the IL-17/IL-23 axis in scalp, nail, and palmoplantar psoriasis: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Scalp, nail, and palmoplantar psoriasis are termed "difficult-to-treat sites" owing to their unique anatomical features and therapeutic resistance, substantially impairing patient quality of life. Although anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 biologics are widely used, head-to-head comparative evidence for achieving high-level lesion clearance at these specific sites remains limited.

Methods

Following PRISMA-NMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and other databases from inception through November 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Primary outcomes were defined as complete or near-complete clearance. Frequentist network meta-analysis was performed to calculate odds ratios (ORs), with treatment rankings derived from surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values.

Results

Twenty-four RCTs involving 5,946 patients and eight biologics plus placebo were included. For palmoplantar psoriasis, secukinumab ranked highest (SUCRA = 79.7%), followed by bimekizumab (72.2%) and ustekinumab (69.7%). For nail psoriasis, bimekizumab ranked first (78.9%), followed by ixekizumab (77.2%) and brodalumab (67.5%); however, local inconsistency for the ixekizumab-placebo comparison and low-certainty evidence warrant caution. For scalp psoriasis, brodalumab (87.7%) and ixekizumab (86.9%) ranked highest, followed by bimekizumab (69.0%) and guselkumab (65.1%); the brodalumab estimate relied on a single contributing study.

Conclusion

During induction-phase follow-up, IL-17 inhibitors tended to rank highly for complete or near-complete clearance at difficult-to-treat psoriasis sites. Bimekizumab and ixekizumab showed consistently favorable rankings across sites, but treatment selection should consider certainty of evidence, sensitivity analyses, long-term response, and patient-level factors.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO, identifier CRD420251271255.

records.title: Target discovery and drug design in the era of artificial intelligence.
records.publisher: Medicinal chemistry research : an international journal for rapid communications on design and mechanisms of action of biologically active agents

content.title: Target discovery and drug design in the era of artificial intelligence.
content.abstract: The identification of therapeutically actionable targets and the design of effective small-molecule modulators remain central challenges in drug discovery, particularly for complex diseases driven by dynamic, interconnected molecular networks. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are reshaping this landscape by enabling integrative analysis of large-scale biological data, systematic navigation of chemical space, and data-driven optimization of molecular properties. In this review, we outline how AI transforms small-molecule drug discovery by linking target discovery, tractability assessment, and chemical design within integrated, experiment-informed workflows. We highlight AI-enabled strategies for target discovery that integrate network biology, multimodal data fusion, and perturbation-aware modeling. These approaches identify context-specific, functionally actionable targets, including non-enzymatic proteins, protein-protein interactions, and other historically challenging classes. We then focus on advances most relevant to medicinal chemistry, including structure and complex prediction, docking and affinity modeling, ligand-based learning, generative molecular design, ADMET prediction, and synthetic feasibility assessment. Finally, we discuss current limitations related to data quality, generalizability, interpretability, and experimental translation. We emphasize the critical future role of integrated, context-aware AI workflows that connect target discovery with chemical design and experimental feedback. Together, these advances position AI as a robust framework for accelerating the discovery of therapeutically relevant targets and small-molecule modulators.

records.title: Governing Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: A Systematic Review of Ethical, Legal, and Regulatory Frameworks.

content.title: Governing Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: A Systematic Review of Ethical, Legal, and Regulatory Frameworks.
content.abstract: Purpose: This systematic review explores the ethical, legal, and regulatory frameworks governing the deployment of artificial intelligence technologies in radiology. It aims to identify key governance challenges and highlight strategies that promote the safe, transparent, and accountable integration of artificial intelligence in clinical imaging. This review is intended for both medical practitioners and AI developers, offering clinicians a synthesis of ethical and legal considerations while providing developers with regulatory insights and guidance for future AI system design. Methods: A systematic review was conducted, examining thirty-eight peer-reviewed articles published between 2018 and 2025. Studies were identified through searches in PubMed, Scopus, and Embase using terms related to artificial intelligence, radiology, ethics, law, and regulation. The inclusion criteria focused on studies addressing governance implications, rather than technical design. A thematic content analysis was applied to identify common patterns and gaps across ethical, legal, and regulatory domains. Results: The findings reveal widespread radiology-specific concerns, including algorithmic bias in breast and chest imaging datasets, opacity in image-based AI systems such as pulmonary nodule detection models, and unresolved legal liability in cases where radiologists rely on FDA-cleared AI tools that fail to identify abnormalities. Regulatory frameworks vary significantly across regions with limited global harmonization, highlighting the need for adaptive oversight models and improved data governance. Conclusion: Responsible deployment of AI in radiology requires governance models that address bias, explainability, and medico-legal accountability while integrating ethical principles, legal safeguards, and adaptive oversight. This review provides tailored insights for medical practitioners, AI developers, policymakers, and researchers: clinicians gain guidance on ethical and legal responsibilities, developers on regulatory and design priorities, policymakers (especially in the Middle East) on regional framework gaps, and researchers on future directions.

records.title: AI-enabled precision evaluation of adrenal masses: radiomics, deep learning, and explainable imaging biomarkers.

content.title: AI-enabled precision evaluation of adrenal masses: radiomics, deep learning, and explainable imaging biomarkers.
content.abstract: Accurate evaluation of adrenal masses remains a significant challenge in endocrinology and radiology, as differential diagnosis involves a wide spectrum of benign and malignant lesions. Radiomics and deep learning (DL) have emerged as promising tools to enhance the precision of adrenal mass assessment by extracting high-dimensional imaging features and enabling automated, data-driven analysis. This review summarizes the latest advancements in the application of radiomics and DL techniques for adrenal mass evaluation. We systematically describe the workflow of radiomic feature extraction and model development, emphasizing their roles in differentiating key lesions such as pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas (PPGLs), adrenal cortical adenomas, and adrenal cortical carcinomas. Additionally, the utility of these approaches in genotype prediction and prognostic evaluation is highlighted. The review further explores the advantages and potential of DL, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), in automated segmentation, feature learning, and end-to-end diagnostic frameworks. Finally, current challenges including technical limitations, clinical translation barriers, and future research directions are discussed, aiming to provide a theoretical foundation for constructing intelligent and precise adrenal mass evaluation systems.

records.title: Effect of laryngeal mask airway versus endotracheal intubation on survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Effect of laryngeal mask airway versus endotracheal intubation on survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To compare the effectiveness and safety of laryngeal mask airway (LMA) versus endotracheal intubation (ETI) on resuscitation outcomes in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).

Methods

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were searched in PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and CBM from database inception to May 31, 2025. The methodological quality and risk of bias of the included RCTs were evaluated with the Cochrane ROB2 tool. We employed RevMan 5.3 and TSA software for all statistical analyses, including meta-analysis, sensitivity analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA). The certainty of the evidence was graded according to the GRADE approach. The primary outcomes included airway establishment time and CPR success rate, and the secondary outcomes included first-attempt intubation success rate, mortality, survival rate, left ventricular ejection fraction, and adverse events.

Results

Nineteen RCTs (11,982 patients) were included. Compared with ETI, LMA was associated with a significantly shorter airway establishment time (MD: -86.95 s; 95% CI: -103.00, -70.90; p < 0.00001), higher first-attempt success rate (RR: 1.44; 95% CI: 1.32, 1.58; p < 0.00001), improved CPR success rate (RR: 1.44; 95% CI: 1.25, 1.67; p < 0.00001), and LVEF (SMD: 1.57; 95% CI: 0.65, 2.48; p < 0.00001). No significant differences were observed in survival rate (RR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.88, 1.09; p = 0.69), nor mortality (RR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.99, 1.01; p = 0.69). LMA was associated with a lower rate of vocal cord injury (RR: 0.11; 95% CI: 0.03, 0.47; p = 0.003), although this finding is based on a small number of events and should be interpreted cautiously. The quality of the GRADE evidence ranged from very low to high.

Conclusion

Compared with ETI, LMA demonstrates significantly higher operational efficiency and a favorable safety profile in the management of OHCA. However, given that survival and mortality outcomes are comparable between the two strategies, LMA may be considered a reasonable alternative to ETI, particularly when minimizing interruptions in chest compressions is a priority or when ETI expertise is limited. The choice of airway device should be individualized rather than uniformly prioritized. In summary, LMA may offer procedural advantages and fewer airway-related complications, while evidence for a survival benefit remains insufficient.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD42025645299, identifier (CRD42025645299).

records.title: Bridging Technology and Nutrition: A Systematic Review of AI and XR Applications for Nutritional Insights in Restaurants and Foodservice Operations.

content.title: Bridging Technology and Nutrition: A Systematic Review of AI and XR Applications for Nutritional Insights in Restaurants and Foodservice Operations.
content.abstract: Purpose: This study provides a critical examination of the literature on applying artificial intelligence (AI) and Extended Reality (XR) in restaurant settings and related foodservice operations. It focuses on how AI and XE influence consumer nutrition awareness and decision-making about food choices, and their implications for customer satisfaction, loyalty, and service delivery in foodservice environments. Design/methodology/approach: The study adopts a systematic literature review (SLR) approach following the PRISMA method. An initial search identified over 3900 academic papers published between 2016 and 2025. Studies were selected on the basis of predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and 26 peer-reviewed articles were analyzed. The review provides a conceptual synthesis and develops propositions for practical applications and future research directions. Findings: The review reveals a shift from static systems that rely on optimization, toward adaptive and user-centered solutions that are behavior-oriented. AI applications predominate in the case of calorie tracking, personalized recommendations, and menu planning. Though deployment of XR technologies (e.g., AR and VR) is less prevalent, they offer potential for immersive, and real-time interventions. A key distinction emerges between studies demonstrating empirical effectiveness (e.g., improved understanding and healthier choices) and those focused on technical and/or conceptual developments. To date, there has been limited validation of behavioral impacts in foodservice settings. Originality: This study offers a theory-informed conceptualization of AI and XR applications in restaurant and foodservice contexts by integrating three perspectives: hospitality (menus and dining experience), nutrition (dietary awareness and healthier choices), and human-technology interaction (technology acceptance and user engagement). The study reconceptualizes AI- and XR-enabled systems as behavioral intervention tools and outlines a focused research agenda for advancing nutritional communication in foodservice environments.

records.title: Closed-loop artificial intelligence agents for animal epidemic prediction and decision support in livestock farming: a review.

content.title: Closed-loop artificial intelligence agents for animal epidemic prediction and decision support in livestock farming: a review.
content.abstract: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception-decision-feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight.

records.title: Cytoflavin's neuroprotective effect in acute ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Cytoflavin's neuroprotective effect in acute ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains a leading cause of long-term disability globally. While reperfusion therapies are effective, there is a growing need for adjunct neuroprotective strategies to minimize secondary brain injury. Cytoflavin, a metabolic and antioxidant compound, has shown potential neuroprotective effects. However, its clinical efficacy remains underexplored. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the efficacy of Cytoflavin in AIS, focusing on neurological recovery (NIHSS), functional independence (Barthel Index), cognitive performance (MMSE), and infarct volume. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases for studies evaluating Cytoflavin in AIS. Nine studies were included, with a combined enrollment of 3,254 participants across treatment arms (sample sizes reported per arm); the number of unique participants contributing to each pooled outcome was smaller after correcting for shared control groups and repeated-measures overlap across evaluation time points (e.g., 1,379 for NIHSS). Data were analyzed using random-effects models; where a shared control group was compared against two Cytoflavin dose arms within the same study, the control group was split proportionally between the two comparisons to avoid double-counting participants (unit-of-analysis correction). Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Cytoflavin significantly improved NIHSS scores (MD = -2.63, 95% CI: -3.15 to -2.10; moderate certainty) and Barthel Index (MD = 19.29, 95% CI: 9.52 to 29.07; moderate certainty), and showed improvements of low certainty in MMSE scores (MD = +6.93, 95% CI: 1.39 to 12.47) and mRS scores (MD = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.74 to -0.09), the latter derived from continuous summary statistics for an inherently ordinal scale (see Limitations). For infarct volume, effects diverged by evaluation time point: a marginal increase was observed at Day-10 (MD = +0.17 cm3, based on a single study), while a non-significant reduction was observed at Day-21 (MD = -4.73 cm3, 95% CI: -11.41 to 1.95; very low certainty). High heterogeneity (I2 ranging from 0% to 100%) was observed across outcomes and persisted after the unit-of-analysis correction, indicating genuine clinical and methodological diversity across studies. In conclusion, cytoflavin shows promising neuroprotective effects in AIS. However, due to heterogeneity and methodological limitations, further large-scale, high-quality studies are needed to confirm its efficacy and optimize treatment protocols. Systematic review registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251112430, identifier: CRD420251112430.

records.title: Real-World Luspatercept Evidence in Myelodysplastic Neoplasms: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Real-World Luspatercept Evidence in Myelodysplastic Neoplasms: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Luspatercept has emerged as a therapeutic option for patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS). Nonetheless, the performance of luspatercept outside of controlled clinical trials remains unclear. We aimed to synthesize real-world evidence (RWE) on the effectiveness and safety of luspatercept. This study was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. We searched for studies up to June 2025 evaluating luspatercept in adult MDS patients. Data on hematologic improvement-erythroid (HI-E), transfusion independence (TI at 8, 12, and 16 weeks), adverse events, and overall survival (OS) were extracted. Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses were performed using priors derived from pooled clinical trials. Seventeen studies were included: five clinical trials (440 patients) and twelve real-world cohorts (1821 patients). The pooled estimate for HI-E was 46.6% (95% CrI: 32.5%-63.9%). For TI, pooled rates at 8, 12, and 16 weeks were 44.7% (95% CrI: 28.6%-61.5%), 38.6% (95% CrI: 21.1%-60.0%), and 30.9% (95% CrI: 10.7%-53.9%), respectively. The subgroups with highest TI and HI-E were patients with positive SF3B1 status (58.5%, at 8 weeks) and Asian patients (54.8%), respectively. Male sex was associated with lower HI-E, 8, and 12 weeks TI rates. Hypertension and falls were more frequently reported in RWE. We estimated OS rates of 88.9% at 1 year and 74.4% at 2 years following treatment initiation. Real-world HI-E were modestly attenuated, likely reflecting selection, adherence, and monitoring differences. The response seems dependent on disease, geographical, and demographical moderators. Such aspects should be taken into account in the design of future studies and in clinical decisions.

records.title: Sugammadex versus anticholinesterase reversal of neuromuscular blockade in adult surgical patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Sugammadex versus anticholinesterase reversal of neuromuscular blockade in adult surgical patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Residual neuromuscular blockade after general anaesthesia is a cause of postoperative pulmonary complications and delayed recovery. Sugammadex, a relaxant-binding agent, is a fast-acting antidote for aminosteroid neuromuscular block which works through encapsulation, in contrast to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine. This study evaluated the effectiveness, postoperative recovery and complications associated with sugammadex versus conventional anticholinesterase reversal drugs in adult surgical patients.

Method

This systematic review and meta-analysis was done based on the PRISMA 2020 statement. Databases like PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus were used to search the literature from January 2000 to December 2025. Studies comparing the use of sugammadex to anticholinesterase agents in adult surgical patients were included, both randomised and non-randomised. Two independent reviewers screened, extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Analyses were carried out in RevMan 5.3 software using random-effect models; the odds ratio (OR) for dichotomous outcomes and the mean difference (MD) for continuous outcomes were used with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Evidence certainty was assessed using the GRADE approach.

Results

Total of ten studies (n = 4,082) were included; 5 randomised control trials and 5 observational studies. There was no statistically significant reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications with sugammadex compared to anticholinesterase (3 studies, n = 688; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47-1.20; p = 0.23; I2 = 77%). There was faster recovery of neuromuscular function with sugammadex, however, there was very high heterogeneity among the studies and the pooled estimate cannot be interpreted as one single effect size (2 studies; I2 = 100%). Recovery time after surgery was reduced (3 studies, n = 260; MD -6.66 min, 95% CI -6.96 to -6.35; p < 0.00001; I2 = 87%) and time to first bowel movement was also earlier (2 studies, n = 559; MD -13.81 h, 95% CI -19.16 to -8.45; p < 0.00001; I2 = 0%). There were no statistically significant differences for PACU stay (MD 1.55 min, 95% CI -1.60 to 4.69), readmission rate (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.62-1.39) and postoperative nausea/vomiting (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.48-1.56).

Conclusion

Faster neuromuscular recovery, shorter recovery time after surgery and early return of bowel function was associated with the use of sugammadex rather than the anticholinesterase agents. There were no differences found for postoperative pulmonary complications, PACU stay, readmission rate or nausea and vomiting. These results are based on small number of clinically heterogeneous studies, in which only 2-4 studies were used in pooling and thus should be considered as preliminary results.

Systematic review registered

CRD420261364292.

records.title: Islet function impairment outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Islet function impairment outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICPis) are associated with islet function impairment (IFI), manifesting as hyperglycemia, diabetes mellitus (DM), or diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Delayed detection and management may lead to irreversible β-cell damage and life-threatening complications. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the risk of IFI associated with ICPis.

Methods

Following PICOS principles, we searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, CNKI, Wanfang, CBM, and VIP databases from inception to October 24, 2024. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ICPis versus non-ICPis regimens in cancer patients. Outcomes included hyperglycemia, DM, and DKA. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using fixed- or random-effects models. Quality was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and publication bias was evaluated by Begg's test. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025639629).

Results

A total of 31 RCT studies with 15,417 patients were included in this study. Results showed that ICPis treatment significantly increased the risk of associated IFI (RR = 1.30, 95%CI: 1.10-1.53, P = 0.002), the risk of grade 3-5 (RR = 2.20, 95%CI: 1.50-3.23, P < 0.0001) and type 1 diabetes (T1DM) (RR = 3.38, 95%CI: 1.66-6.88, P = 0.0008) compared to those treated with non-ICPis; Subgroup analysis showed that, compared with non-ICPis, the PD-1 inhibitor and Pembrolizumab groups significantly increased the incidence of developing IFI (RR = 1.57, 95%CI: 1.22-2.01, P = 0.0005; RR = 2.38, 95%CI: 1.43-3.97, P = 0.0009); Patients with NSCLC receiving ICPis had a significantly higher risk of developing IFI compared with non-ICPis (RR = 1.32, 95%CI: 1.01-1.72, P = 0.04). Compared to their respective non-ICPis controls, the point estimate for IFI risk was lower with ICPis plus chemotherapy (RR = 1.23) than with ICPis monotherapy (RR = 1.43); a similar pattern was observed for grade 3-5 IFI (RR = 1.53 vs. 3.39). No publication bias was detected.

Conclusions

ICPis significantly increase the risk of IFI, particularly T1DM and severe (grade 3-5) events. PD-1 inhibitors and patients with NSCLC represent high-risk subgroups. We strongly recommend multidisciplinary monitoring and proactive blood glucose management.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/myprospero, identifier CRD42025639629.

records.title: A meta-analysis of influencing factors of non-suicidal self-injury behavior in adolescents with depression.

content.title: A meta-analysis of influencing factors of non-suicidal self-injury behavior in adolescents with depression.
content.abstract:
Aim

This study aimed to analyze the influencing factors of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) in adolescents with depression.

Methods

This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) for observational studies on factors influencing NSSI behavior in adolescents with depression published between 1 January 2010 and 7 May 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Meta-analyses were performed in RevMan 5.4 using mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals. Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using the χ² test and I² statistic, and fixed- or random-effects models were applied as appropriate.

Results

In total, 11 studies were included, involving 529 patients in the study group and 1,716 patients in the control group. The meta-analysis showed that, compared with the control group, the study group had significantly higher scores for interpersonal problems, negative emotions, alexithymia, and negative self-esteem [MD = 5.88, 95% CI (3.19, 8.57), P < 0.001], somatic symptom scores [MD = 5.20, 95% CI (-0.03, 10.43), P = 0.05], emotional deficit [MD = 6.82, 95% CI (0.32, 13.31), P = 0.04], Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores [MD = 2.97, 95% CI (1.76, 4.18), P < 0.001], emotional abuse [MD = 2.10, 95% CI (1.06, 3.13), P < 0.001], physical abuse [MD = 0.64, 95% CI (0.08, 1.20), P = 0.025], sexual abuse [MD = 0.27, 95% CI (0.12, 0.42), P < 0.001], emotional neglect [MD = 1.67, 95% CI (0.37, 2.97), P = 0.009], physical neglect [MD = 0.81, 95% CI (0.43, 1.19), P < 0.001], and Childhood Trauma Questionnaire total scores [MD = 8.93, 95% CI (3.63, 14.24), P < 0.001].

Conclusion

Adolescents with depressive disorders and NSSI tend to exhibit more severe depressive symptoms, maladaptive emotional regulation patterns, negative coping styles, and higher levels of childhood trauma exposure than those without NSSI. These psychosocial and emotional factors may play important roles in the occurrence and maintenance of NSSI behaviors. Early psychological assessment and targeted intervention may help reduce the risk of NSSI in adolescents with depressive disorders.

records.title: Effect of social media-based diabetes self-management education and support on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare

content.title: Effect of social media-based diabetes self-management education and support on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Digital interventions are being used for diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES), but evidence of their effectiveness is limited. This review and meta-analysis examined the impact of social media-based DSMES on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), and an exploratory post hoc analysis assessed the effect of intervention duration on outcomes.

Methods

A PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was conducted using PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PsycINFO, with 789 records screened and one additional record identified through a saved search (total of 790). Eligible studies were English-language articles published over a just-over-ten-year period. These studies focused on adults with T2DM, reported HbA1c outcomes, and utilized social media for DSMES interventions. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). A random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled mean differences (MD) in HbA1c percentage points, with subgroup analyses by intervention duration; heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic.

Results

This systematic review identified 13 studies, including 11 RCTs for the meta-analysis. The pooled analysis demonstrated a statistically significant overall effect favoring the intervention (MD = -0.44 HbA1c percentage points, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.00, p = 0.05). Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed (I² = 91%), and the 95% prediction interval ranged from -2.08 to 1.20. Interventions of 3 months or less showed no significant effect (MD = -0.12, 95%CI -0.51 to 0.28, p = .56), whereas interventions longer than three months showed a large, statistically significant effect (MD = -1.02, 95% CI -1.75 to -0.29, p = 0.01). The test for between-subgroup differences was significant (Q = 4.56, df = 1, p = .03).

Conclusion

Social media-based DSMES interventions may be associated with improvements in glycemic outcomes in adults with T2DM. While interventions longer than three months showed greater pooled effects, interpret these post hoc results carefully because of significant heterogeneity (I² = 91%). This pooled estimate represents an average effect across heterogeneous interventions and populations and therefore should not be understood as a uniform effect of social media-based DSMES.

Systematic review registration

https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BZR6P, OSF Registries BZR6P.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in headache medicine: between automation and the doctor-patient relationship. A systematic review.
records.publisher: The journal of headache and pain

content.title: Artificial intelligence in headache medicine: between automation and the doctor-patient relationship. A systematic review.
content.abstract:
Background

Headache disorders, particularly migraine, are highly prevalent, but often remain underdiagnosed and undertreated. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promising applications in diagnosis, prediction of attacks, analysis of neuroimaging and neurophysiology data, and treatment selection. Its use in headache medicine raises ethical, regulatory, and clinical questions, including its impact on the doctor-patient relationship.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted on April 10, 2025, across PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and DOAJ, following PRISMA guidelines. Two reviewers independently applied strict inclusion criteria to select studies published from 2000 to 2025 in either English or Spanish. Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools tailored to study design, including the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2), Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST), Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), and Appraisal Tool for Cross-Sectional Studies (AXIS).

Results

A total of 76 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. The analysis covered AI methodologies, clinical applications, patient perspectives, and ethical implications. AI tools have shown potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, headache subtype classification, and prediction of treatment response, and may help reduce the administrative burden in clinical practice. Emerging technologies such as digital twins, wearable biomarker monitoring, and synthetic data generation support personalized approaches and may reshape clinical research. However, significant challenges remain. These include data quality, model interpretability, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and regulatory gaps. Moreover, the evidence base is still developing, with expectations often exceeding the strength of available clinical data. Many studies present methodological limitations due to small sample sizes, selection bias, and lack of external validation, which limit their generalizability to real-world settings. Finally, concerns about depersonalization and transparency affect patient trust in AI, reinforcing the need for both human oversight and a patient-centered approach.

Conclusions

AI holds promise for improving headache care, but evidence supporting its clinical utility is still limited. Integration into practice must be rigorously validated, ethically guided, and carefully designed to prevent depersonalization. Human oversight remains essential as AI should complement, not replace, clinical judgment.

records.title: Roadmap for inferring metabolic regulation using multiomics, machine learning, and genome-scale modeling.

content.title: Roadmap for inferring metabolic regulation using multiomics, machine learning, and genome-scale modeling.
content.abstract: Machine learning and genome-scale metabolic modeling have accelerated the discovery of metabolic-regulatory relationships in model microbes and mammalian cells. This review provides a roadmap for integrating omics with computational methods for studying systems-level transcriptional, post-translational, and allosteric regulation. Developing methods to infer and integrate multiple regulatory mechanisms simultaneously is essential for discovering novel modes of metabolic regulation and precise engineering of metabolic networks.

records.title: Comparative effects of exercise modalities on depression, anxiety, and stress in university students: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

content.title: Comparative effects of exercise modalities on depression, anxiety, and stress in university students: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To compare the effects of different exercise interventions on depression, anxiety, and stress in university students and to identify outcome-specific patterns and relevant prescription features using network meta-analysis.

Methods

A systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to 31 October 2025. Eligible studies included university students aged 18 years or older, structured exercise interventions lasting at least 4 weeks, and validated measures of depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, or perceived stress. Pairwise random-effects meta-analyses and random-effects network meta-analyses were performed. Effects were summarized as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), and treatments were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve.

Results

Twenty-five RCTs involving 2,127 students were included. Compared with control conditions, exercise was associated with improvements in depression (SMD -1.07, 95% CI -1.38 to -0.75; I 2 = 87.6%), anxiety (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.38; I 2 = 87.1%), and stress (SMD -0.45, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.16; I 2 = 75.2%). These effects should be interpreted cautiously due to substantial heterogeneity and variation in outcome measures. Network meta-analysis indicated outcome-specific patterns: mind-body exercise and aerobic exercise were most consistently associated with favorable outcomes for depression; mind-body exercise showed clearer associations for anxiety, whereas team sports and resistance-based approaches appeared favorable but were supported by limited evidence; aerobic exercise was linked to the strongest comparative effect for stress. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that sessions of 30-59 min were more frequently associated with benefits for depression and anxiety, whereas stress benefits were more often observed with sessions of 30 min or longer. Moderate to vigorous intensity and higher weekly frequency were associated with more favorable anxiety and stress outcomes, although these findings should be considered exploratory rather than definitive.

Conclusion

Exercise interventions are associated with improvements in depression, anxiety, and stress in university students, with outcome-specific patterns varying by modality. Exploratory findings suggest that time-efficient, moderate to vigorous exercise could inform future research on student mental health promotion.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261379734.

records.title: Effects and potential mechanisms of <i>si-ni-san</i> on animal models of depression: a preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effects and potential mechanisms of <i>si-ni-san</i> on animal models of depression: a preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Context

In Traditional Chinese Medicine depressive disorders are commonly associated with liver qi stagnation syndrome. Si-ni-san (SNS), a classic formula for soothing the liver and relieving qi stagnation, is widely used for its potential antidepressant-like effects.

Objective

This preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the pharmacological effects of SNS on depression-related behavioral outcomes in animal models and to summarize its mechanisms of action.

Methods

We conducted a systematic search of seven databases (including PubMed) for records published up to December 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE's tool. Meta-analyses were performed using STATA 15.0 and RevMan 5.4. Subgroup and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the findings. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's test. Trim-and-fill analysis was performed to adjust for potential publication bias. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using a modified GRADE approach for preclinical studies.

Results

A total of 28 studies were included, involving 384 animals and three behavioral tests: sucrose preference test (SPT), forced swim test (FST), and tail suspension test (TST). SNS treatment was associated with increased sucrose preference in the SPT (SMD = 3.18, 95% CI = [2.44, 3.93]), and reduced immobility time in both the FST (SMD = -2.17, 95% CI = [-2.86, -1.49]) and TST (SMD = -2.55, 95% CI = [-3.31, -1.78]). Mechanistically, SNS treatment was associated with increased monoamine neurotransmitters (MNTs), reduced hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hormones, and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Conclusion

These findings suggest that SNS is associated with antidepressant-like pharmacological effects in rodent models, with changes in MNTs, HPA axis hormones, and inflammatory markers. However, due to substantial heterogeneity, risk of bias, and inadequate phytochemical characterization, these results should be considered hypothesis-generating and interpreted with caution.

records.title: AI in Medical Questionnaires: Scoping Review

content.title: AI in Medical Questionnaires: Scoping Review
content.abstract:
This systematic review aimed to explore the current applications, potential benefits, and issues of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical questionnaires, focusing on its role in 3 main functions: assessment, development, and prediction. The global mental health burden remains severe. The World Health Organization reports that >1 billion people worldwide experience mental disorders, with the prevalence of depression and anxiety among children and adolescents at 2.6% and 6.5%, respectively. However, commonly used clinical questionnaires such as the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Beck Depression Inventory suffer from several problems, including the high degree of overlap of symptoms of depression with those of other psychiatric disorders and a lack of professional supervision during administration of the questionnaires, which often lead to inaccurate diagnoses. In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, the health care system is facing the dual challenges of a surge in patient numbers and the complexity of mental health issues. AI technology has now been shown to have great promise in improving diagnostic accuracy, assisting clinical decision-making, and simplifying questionnaire development and data analysis. To systematically assess the value of AI in medical questionnaires, this study searched 5 databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure) for the period from database inception to September 2024. Of 49,091 publications, a total of 14 (0.03%) studies met the inclusion criteria. AI technologies showed significant advantages in assessment, such as distinguishing myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome from long COVID-19 with 92.18% accuracy. In questionnaire development, natural language processing using generative models such as ChatGPT was used to construct culturally competent scales. In terms of disease prediction, one study had an area under the curve of 0.790 for cataract surgery risk prediction.
